0.title: Who Jesus Is and What He Has Done
0.overview:
Jesus once asked his disciples, But who do you say that I am? (Matt 16:15). Every person who has ever heard of him must answer the same question. Some say he was a good teacher, a prophet, a revolutionary or a legend. Peter answered, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matt 16:16), and Jesus said that answer came from the Father himself.

Christianity is not first a set of ideas or a way of life. It is a person. Take Christ out of Christianity and nothing is left. Everything the Bible says about salvation depends on two questions: who is Jesus, and what has he done? If he is not God, he cannot save us. If he is not truly man, he cannot stand in our place. If he did not die for our sins, we are still in them. If he did not rise, our faith is futile (1 Cor 15:17).

This study looks at both: the person of Christ (who he is) and the work of Christ (what he has done, is doing and will do). The two belong together. Only someone who is both God and man could do what Jesus did. And what he did shows us who he is.

Six units: (1) The Word Became Flesh; (2) Truly God and Truly Man; (3) Prophet, Priest and King; (4) The Cross: Christ Our Substitute; (5) Risen, Ascended and Reigning; (6) He Will Come Again. The aim is not only to understand Christ better but to love and trust him more.

1.title: The Word Became Flesh
1.overview:
John's Gospel does not begin in Bethlehem. It begins before creation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). The one who would be born of Mary already existed. He was with God, distinct from the Father. And he was God, sharing the Father's nature. Through him all things were made (John 1:3).

Then comes the most astonishing sentence ever written: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The eternal Son of God took to himself a full human nature, a real body and a real human soul. He did not stop being God. He did not merely appear human or borrow a body for a while. He became what he was not, while remaining what he was. This is the incarnation.

The virgin birth. Both Matthew and Luke record that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of Mary, a virgin. Mary herself asked, How will this be, since I am a virgin? The angel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her, therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God (Luke 1:34-35). The virgin birth is not a decorative miracle. It marks Jesus as a new beginning, the second Adam, truly human through Mary, yet not simply one more child of Adam's line. Salvation comes from above, not from human achievement.

Why the incarnation? Scripture gives several answers. He came to reveal the Father: No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known (John 1:18). He came to save: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Tim 1:15). He came to share our nature so that he could die in our place and defeat death (Heb 2:14). And he came to be a merciful high priest who understands our weakness (Heb 2:17).

The humility of it. Paul says Christ, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:6-7). The Lord of glory was born in a borrowed stable, grew up in an obscure town and worked with his hands. He came down so that we could be lifted up.
1.theology:
"He emptied himself": the views. Some modern teachers, reading Philippians 2:7, have argued that the Son laid aside some of his divine attributes, such as his knowledge or power, in order to become man. On this view, Jesus was not fully God while on earth. Historic Christianity holds that the Son laid aside not his divine nature but his divine glory and privileges, by adding a human nature and taking the place of a servant.

The verdict: Paul explains how Christ emptied himself: by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men (Phil 2:7). The emptying was by addition, not subtraction. God cannot stop being God. Even on earth, Jesus calmed storms, forgave sins and knew people's thoughts. Yet in his human nature he grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and, by his own choice, lived in dependence on the Father and the Spirit.

Eternal Son: The Son did not become the Son at Bethlehem. He is the eternal Son of the eternal Father. And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed (John 17:5).
1.examples:
Then: The shepherds near Bethlehem were among the lowest of society. Yet the angels came to them, and the sign they were given was a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger (Luke 2:12). The Saviour of the world was announced to nobodies and found in a feeding trough.

Now: A Christian who has always thought of Christmas as a sentimental holiday reads John 1:1-14 slowly in December. The baby in the nativity scene is the one through whom all things were made. Christmas stops being a pleasant festival and becomes a staggering fact: God came near.

A simple test: When you picture Jesus, do you picture him as truly God, as truly man, or as both? Most of us lean one way. Scripture holds both.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John deliberately echoes Genesis 1:1. Before anything was created, the Word already was. He was with God, a distinct person. He was God, of the same nature. And he was the Creator: nothing that exists was made without him. Jesus is not the highest creature. He is the one through whom all creatures came to be.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two words carry the weight: became and dwelt. The Word became flesh, real humanity. And he dwelt among us, pitching his tent like God's presence in the tabernacle in the wilderness. The glory that once filled the tabernacle was now seen in a man, full of grace and truth. To see Jesus is to see God's glory up close.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to her, "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." And Mary said to the angel, "How will this be, since I am a virgin?" And the angel answered her, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Gabriel's message to Mary joins two lines of promise. Jesus will be given the throne of his father David: he is the long-promised King. And he will be called the Son of God: he is more than a king. His conception by the Holy Spirit is the reason. Mary's son is David's son and God's Son at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul writes this to stop quarrels in a church. The answer to selfishness is the mind of Christ. The one who had every right to glory chose the lowest place, all the way down to death on a cross, the most shameful death the Roman world knew. If the Son of God made himself nothing for us, we can surely put others first.

1.reflection:
Read John 1:1-18. What does each verse tell you about who Jesus is?

Why does it matter that Jesus was born of a virgin?

How would you explain Philippians 2:7 to someone who thinks Jesus gave up being God?

Where is God calling you to imitate the humility of Christ this week?

2.title: Truly God and Truly Man
2.overview:
Who is Jesus? The New Testament answers with two truths that must never be separated: he is fully God and fully man, one person forever.

Truly God. The New Testament calls Jesus God directly. Thomas, falling at the risen Christ's feet, said, My Lord and my God! (John 20:28), and Jesus accepted it. Paul writes, in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Col 2:9). Jesus does what only God can do: he creates (Col 1:16), sustains the universe (Heb 1:3), forgives sins (Mark 2:5-7), raises the dead (John 5:21) and will judge the world (John 5:22). He receives worship (Matt 14:33; Heb 1:6), which God gives to no creature. And he claims God's own name: before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). His hearers understood him, because they picked up stones to throw at him.

Truly man. Jesus was not God in disguise. He was born, grew up, learned, worked, ate, slept and got tired. He was thirsty at the well and wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 4:6-7; 11:35). He felt sorrow, anger, compassion and joy. He was in every respect... tempted as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15). He died a real death and was raised with a real body, which he still has.

One person. Jesus is not two persons, a divine one and a human one, sharing a body. He is one person, the eternal Son, who has two natures. Whatever either nature does, the one person does. That is why Paul can say that the rulers crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8). God did not die in his divine nature, which cannot die. But the one who died was God the Son, in his human nature.

Why both matter. Only a man could die for men; only God could make that death infinitely valuable and conquer death. Only a man could be our example and our sympathising priest; only God could be our Saviour and Lord. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). The bridge must reach both banks.
2.theology:
The church's confession: In AD 451, at the Council of Chalcedon, the church summarised the biblical teaching. Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, "without confusion" (the natures are not mixed into something new), "without change," "without division" and "without separation." This was not new teaching. It was a fence around the mystery the New Testament already reveals.

Errors on every side: Some, ancient and modern, deny that Jesus is fully God, making him a created being, however exalted. Jehovah's Witnesses teach this today. Others deny that he is fully human, making his body or his human mind an illusion. Others divide him into two persons, or blend the natures into a third thing. Each error destroys salvation, because each removes either the God who saves or the man who stands in our place.

Without sin: Christ's sinlessness does not make him less human. Sin is not part of what it means to be human; it is a corruption of it. Jesus is the truest human who ever lived.
2.examples:
Then: In a storm on Galilee, Jesus was asleep in the boat, worn out like any man. Woken by terrified disciples, he stood and spoke to the wind and sea, and there was a great calm. The disciples asked, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41). The same scene shows his true humanity and his true deity.

Now: A Jehovah's Witness couple knocks on a Christian's door and says Jesus is "a god" but not God Almighty. Instead of arguing about a single verse, she opens John 20:28 and Hebrews 1:8-10 and asks, "If Jesus is not God, why does the Father call him God and Creator?" The conversation goes deeper than either side expected.

A simple test: Do you bring your weaknesses to Jesus as someone who understands them? Do you worship him as someone who rules over them? Both are right.

verseByVerse.quote: Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you." Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe." Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!" Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Thomas had refused to believe without seeing the wounds. Jesus offered them. Thomas's response is the highest confession in the Gospels: My Lord and my God! Jesus does not correct him. He blesses those who will believe the same without seeing. That includes every reader of John's Gospel (John 20:31).

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ. For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Colossians were being drawn toward philosophies that promised a fuller spiritual experience. Paul's answer is that everything is already in Christ. The whole fullness of deity lives in him, and lives bodily, in his risen human body. And believers are filled in him. There is nothing to add to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery. For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Why did the Son become human? To die, and by dying to destroy the devil's power and free those enslaved by the fear of death. He had to be made like his brothers in every respect to be a merciful and faithful high priest. Because he was tempted and suffered, he is able to help those who are tempted.

verseByVerse.quote: Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Our high priest is great, for he has passed through the heavens. And he is sympathetic, for he was tempted in every way as we are. That combination is the reason we can come boldly. We approach a throne, but it is a throne of grace, and the one beside it knows exactly what we face.

2.reflection:
List three things Jesus did that only God can do, and three things that show he was truly human.

Why is it necessary for our salvation that Jesus is both God and man?

How does Hebrews 4:15-16 change the way you pray when you are tempted?

How would you answer someone who says Jesus never claimed to be God?

3.title: Prophet, Priest and King
3.overview:
The title "Christ" is not Jesus' surname. It means "anointed one," the same as the Old Testament word Messiah. In Israel, three kinds of people were anointed or appointed by God to serve him: prophets, priests and kings. Jesus fulfils all three offices perfectly.

Christ the Prophet. Moses promised, The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen (Deut 18:15). Jesus is that prophet (Acts 3:22). But he is more than a prophet. The prophets brought God's word; Jesus is God's Word. Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:1-2). He is God's final and complete word. We listen to him in Scripture.

Christ the Priest. A priest represents people before God and offers sacrifice for their sins. The priests of Israel offered animals again and again, and then died and had to be replaced. Jesus is a better priest in every way. He offered not an animal but himself. He offered once, not repeatedly: he did this once for all when he offered up himself (Heb 7:27). And he lives forever, so he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25). He is both the priest and the sacrifice.

Christ the King. God promised David a son whose throne would last forever (2 Sam 7:12-16). Jesus is that King. He was born King of the Jews (Matt 2:2), entered Jerusalem on a donkey as Zechariah foretold, and was crucified under a sign naming him King. After his resurrection he said, All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matt 28:18). He reigns now at God's right hand, ruling his church by his word and Spirit and ruling all things for its good (Eph 1:22).

The three offices answer our three great needs. We are ignorant, and need a prophet to teach us. We are guilty, and need a priest to reconcile us. We are weak and enslaved, and need a king to rule and defend us. In Christ we have all three.
3.theology:
Humiliation and exaltation: Christ carried out these offices in two stages. In his humiliation he was born in lowliness, lived under the law, suffered, died and was buried. In his exaltation he rose, ascended, sits at God's right hand and will come to judge. Philippians 2:6-11 traces both: down to the cross, then up to the name above every name.

Priest-king like Melchizedek: In Israel, priests came from Levi and kings from Judah; no one could be both. Psalm 110 foresees a King who is also a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (Ps 110:4), like the mysterious priest-king of Genesis 14. Hebrews applies it to Jesus (Heb 7).

No other mediator: Because Christ is our one priest, Christians need no other priest to bring them to God, and no repeated sacrifice. Every believer may come to God directly through him (Heb 10:19-22).
3.examples:
Then: On the road to Emmaus, two disappointed disciples told the unrecognised Jesus that they had hoped he would redeem Israel. He answered, Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:26-27). The whole Old Testament was pointing to him.

Now: A believer is overwhelmed: confused about a decision, guilty over a sin and anxious about forces beyond her control. Her pastor reminds her that Christ is her Prophet to guide her through his word, her Priest who has paid for her sin and prays for her now, and her King who rules over everything she fears.

A simple test: Which of Christ's offices do you most neglect? Do you listen to him, rest in his sacrifice and submit to his rule?

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen— just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, 'Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.' And the LORD said to me, 'They are right in what they have spoken. I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: At Sinai the people were terrified by God's voice and asked for a mediator. God approved and promised a prophet like Moses who would speak his words. The prophets who followed never fully fulfilled this; Deuteronomy itself ends by saying no prophet like Moses had yet arisen (Deut 34:10). Jesus is the one who speaks God's words perfectly, because he is God's Word.

verseByVerse.quote: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world. He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These verses move from prophet to priest to king. God has spoken by his Son. The Son, after making purification for sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. He sat down because his work was finished. The old priests stood daily at their service (Heb 10:11); there was always more to do.

verseByVerse.quote: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them. For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The old priests were many because they kept dying. Jesus holds his priesthood permanently, because he lives forever. So he can save to the uttermost those who come to God through him. He never stops praying for his people. And he needs no daily sacrifices, because his one sacrifice of himself was enough.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool." The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies! Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power, in holy garments; from the womb of the morning, the dew of your youth will be yours. The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the Old Testament passages most often quoted in the New. David hears the LORD speak to my Lord, inviting him to sit at his right hand until his enemies are defeated. Jesus used it to show that the Messiah is more than David's son (Matt 22:41-45). He is David's Lord, the eternal King and eternal Priest.

3.reflection:
Which of the three offices of Christ do you think about least? Why?

How does Christ's ongoing intercession (Heb 7:25) encourage you?

Read Luke 24:13-35. How does Jesus use the Old Testament to explain himself?

What would it look like to submit an area of your life to Christ as King this week?

4.title: The Cross: Christ Our Substitute
4.overview:
The cross is the centre of the Christian faith. The Gospels give a large share of their pages to the last week of Jesus' life. Paul said, I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Cor 2:2). But why did Jesus have to die?

Because of our sin. Sin is not merely a mistake or a weakness. It is rebellion against a holy God, and it deserves his just punishment. The wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23). No amount of good works can pay this debt, because even our best works are stained (Isa 64:6).

Because God loves. The cross was not an accident, nor a tragedy forced on God. It was planned before the world began (Acts 2:23; 1 Pet 1:20). For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son (John 3:16). The Father did not have to be persuaded to love us by the Son. The cross is the expression of his love.

In our place. Isaiah saw it centuries before: But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isa 53:5). Jesus said he came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Peter writes, He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet 2:24). Paul says, Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). The language is consistent: he took what we deserved, so that we could receive what he deserved. This is called penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty of sin as our substitute.

What the cross achieved. The New Testament uses many pictures. It is a sacrifice that removes guilt. It is propitiation, turning away God's wrath (Rom 3:25). It is redemption, paying a ransom to free slaves. It is reconciliation, making enemies friends. It is victory, disarming the powers of evil: God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15). And it is the supreme example of love (1 Pet 2:21). Each picture is true. But beneath them all is substitution: he died in our place.
4.theology:
Views of the atonement: Some teach that the cross was mainly a moral example, showing God's love to move us to repentance. Others stress victory over evil powers. Some reject penal substitution entirely, calling it violent or unjust, as though an angry Father punished an unwilling Son.

The verdict: The example and the victory are both biblical, but neither works without substitution. An example of love saves no one unless the death actually accomplished something for us. And Satan's power over us rests on our guilt; when guilt is removed, his accusations fail (Col 2:14-15). Nor is substitution unjust. The Son was not an unwilling victim: No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The Father, Son and Spirit were united in the plan. And the one who bore the penalty was God himself, in the person of the Son. The judge took the sentence.

For whom did Christ die? The Reformed answer, explained in the Doctrines of Grace study, is that Christ's death actually secured the salvation of all the elect, while being sufficient for all and freely offered to all.
4.examples:
Then: Barabbas was a murderer and rebel, guilty and condemned. The crowd chose him to be released, and Jesus was crucified instead (Mark 15:6-15). Barabbas walked free because another man took his place. Every believer is Barabbas.

Now: A man who has heard about the cross all his life has always thought of it as something sad that happened to Jesus. Reading Isaiah 53 in a modern translation for the first time, he notices the pronouns: our transgressions, our iniquities, we are healed. He realises the cross is not something that happened to Jesus. It is something Jesus did for him.

A simple test: Can you explain in one sentence why Jesus died? Try using the words "for me" and "in my place."

verseByVerse.quote: Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Written centuries before the crucifixion, this is the clearest prophecy of the cross in the Old Testament. Notice the contrast between "he" and "we." We went astray; he was pierced. We had iniquities; he was crushed. We are healed; he was wounded. And above it all stands God's own purpose: the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James and John had just asked for the best seats in the kingdom. Jesus turns their ambition upside down. He came to serve, and the greatest service was to give his life as a ransom, the price paid to free a captive. The phrase for many points to the one dying in the place of the many.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed. For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter writes to slaves suffering unjustly, and points them to Christ as their example. But he cannot speak of Christ's example without going further: Jesus bore our sins in his body on the tree. He is not only the pattern for our suffering; he is the substitute for our sins. And the result is new life: we were straying sheep, now returned to our Shepherd.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul joins two pictures of the cross. First, a debt cancelled: the record against us was nailed to the cross. Second, a victory won: the evil powers were disarmed and shamed, like captives led in a Roman triumph. The two are connected. Once our debt is paid, the accuser has nothing left to accuse us of.

4.reflection:
Why could God not simply forgive sin without the cross?

Read Isaiah 53. Underline every "we," "our" and "us." What do you notice?

How would you answer someone who says penal substitution makes God cruel?

How should the cross shape the way you think about your worst sins?

5.title: Risen, Ascended and Reigning
5.overview:
The story does not end at the tomb. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said (Matt 28:6). On the third day Jesus rose bodily from the dead, and the course of history was changed.

The resurrection is real. The tomb was empty, and even Jesus' enemies did not deny it; they only tried to explain it away (Matt 28:11-15). The risen Jesus appeared many times, to individuals and to groups, once to more than five hundred at once, most of whom were still alive when Paul wrote (1 Cor 15:6). The disciples, who had fled in fear, became bold witnesses willing to suffer for their message. The resurrection is not a myth or a metaphor. It happened.

The resurrection matters. It proves that Jesus is who he said he was: he was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead (Rom 1:4). It shows that the Father accepted his sacrifice: he was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Rom 4:25). It defeats death. And it guarantees our resurrection: Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20), the first sheaf of a harvest that is coming. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Cor 15:17). Everything hangs on Easter.

The ascension. Forty days after his resurrection, Jesus was taken up into heaven before his disciples' eyes (Acts 1:9). This is not his departure from the story but his coronation. He sat down at the right hand of God, the place of supreme authority. From there he poured out the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:33).

What Christ is doing now. He reigns over all things for the sake of his church (Eph 1:20-22). He intercedes for his people: Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us (Rom 8:34). He builds his church through the preaching of the gospel. And he is preparing a place for his people (John 14:2-3). The risen Christ is not absent. He is present by his Spirit and active from his throne.
5.theology:
A real body: The risen Jesus was not a ghost. He invited the disciples to touch him, and he ate fish in front of them (Luke 24:39-43). His body was the same body, bearing the wounds, yet transformed and glorified, no longer subject to death. Our resurrection bodies will be like his (Phil 3:21).

A real man in heaven: The Son did not shed his human nature at the ascension. There is a man on the throne of the universe, and he is our brother. This is why he can sympathise with us and why we will one day be with him bodily.

Union with the risen Christ: Believers are united to Christ in his death and resurrection (Rom 6:4-5). His resurrection life already works in us by the Spirit, giving us power to walk in newness of life, and it will one day raise our bodies.
5.examples:
Then: Peter had denied Jesus three times. After the resurrection, on a beach in Galilee, the risen Lord cooked him breakfast and asked him three times, Do you love me? (John 21:15-17). The resurrection was not only a victory over death. It was the beginning of Peter's restoration.

Now: A widow stands at her husband's graveside. She grieves deeply. But she believes that Christ is the firstfruits, and that her husband's body, like a seed, will be raised. Her tears are real, but so is her hope. She does not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13).

A simple test: What difference would it make to your life this week if the resurrection were not true? If the answer is "very little," you may not yet have seen how much depends on it.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the earliest summaries of the Christian faith, which Paul had received and passed on. It has four parts: Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared. Paul lists witnesses by name and number, as if to say, "Go and ask them." The resurrection is presented as history, open to checking.

verseByVerse.quote: And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied. But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul faces the possibility squarely. If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile, sins are unforgiven, the dead are lost and Christians are the most pitiable people alive. Then comes the great reversal: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead. Christianity stakes everything on one event, and that event happened.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples stand staring at the sky. Two angels redirect them: this same Jesus will come back in the same way, visibly and bodily. The ascension means the disciples should not gaze upward but go outward, as witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8), until he returns.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised— who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Who can condemn a believer? Paul answers with four facts about Christ: he died, he was raised, he is at God's right hand, and he is interceding for us. Each one answers a different accusation. Our security rests not on how well we are doing but on where Christ is and what he is doing.

5.reflection:
Read 1 Corinthians 15:12-20. What would be lost if Christ had not been raised?

How would you summarise the evidence for the resurrection to a sceptical friend?

What difference does it make to you that a real man now sits on the throne of the universe?

How does Christ's intercession for you (Rom 8:34) speak to your fears or guilt?

6.title: He Will Come Again
6.overview:
The same Jesus who ascended will return. The New Testament speaks of the second coming again and again. It is the hope that sustained the early church and the prayer with which the Bible ends: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! (Rev 22:20).

How he will come. Not secretly but visibly: every eye will see him (Rev 1:7). Not as a humble baby but in glory: For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thess 4:16). Not at a predictable date but suddenly: concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matt 24:36). Jesus warned his followers not to be misled by those who claim to know.

What will happen. The dead will be raised, believers and unbelievers alike (John 5:28-29). Believers still alive will be transformed and caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thess 4:17). Christ will judge the world in righteousness: God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed (Acts 17:31). The man who was judged at Pilate's court will be the Judge of all. Then he will make all things new, and his people will live with him forever on a renewed earth (Rev 21:1-5).

Every knee will bow. Because Christ humbled himself, God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Phil 2:9-10). Some will bow in joy, others in defeat. But every one will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

How we wait. The second coming is not a puzzle for speculation but a motive for living. We wait with hope, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (Titus 2:13). We wait with holiness, because everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself (1 John 3:3). We wait with urgency, telling others while there is time. And we wait with comfort, for the Lord we long to see is the Lord who loves us.
6.theology:
One coming, one resurrection, one judgment: Christians hold different views about the order of events at the end, which the End Times Models study sets out. The amillennial reading is the most faithful to Scripture: Christ reigns now, and at his single return there will be a general resurrection of the just and the unjust, the final judgment and the new creation. All orthodox views agree on the central truth: Jesus will return bodily, visibly and gloriously to judge and to save.

Judgment for believers: Believers will stand before Christ, not to be condemned, for there is no condemnation for those in Christ (Rom 8:1), but to have their lives revealed and their faithfulness rewarded (2 Cor 5:10). The Judge is their Saviour.

Christ is the centre of the end: The goal of history is not merely heaven but Christ. Paul's longing was to depart and be with Christ (Phil 1:23). The best thing about the new creation will be that he is there.
6.examples:
Then: The Thessalonian believers were grieving members who had died before Christ returned. Paul did not give them a timetable. He gave them a hope: the dead in Christ will rise first, and we will all be with the Lord forever. Therefore encourage one another with these words (1 Thess 4:18).

Now: A Christian notices that his thoughts about the future are filled with retirement plans, worries about the economy and politics, and almost never with Christ's return. He begins to end his evening prayers with "Come, Lord Jesus." Over time, his anxieties loosen. His future has a face.

A simple test: If Christ returned today, would you be glad? What would you wish you had done differently?

verseByVerse.quote: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope. For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep. For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. Therefore encourage one another with these words. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul writes to comfort grieving believers. Christians grieve, but not without hope. Because Jesus died and rose, those who have died in him will rise. The Lord himself will come, the dead will be raised and the living transformed, and all will be with the Lord forever. The purpose of this teaching is stated plainly: encouragement.

verseByVerse.quote: The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul ends his speech in Athens with a warning. God has overlooked ignorance in the past, but now commands all people everywhere to repent, because a day of judgment is fixed. The Judge is named, and God has given proof by raising him from the dead. The resurrection is not only a comfort; it is a summons.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The one who went down to the cross is lifted to the highest place. Every knee in heaven, on earth and under the earth will bow, and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Isaiah heard God say that every knee would bow to him (Isa 45:23). Paul applies those words to Jesus. And it all ends to the glory of God the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul joins Christ's two comings. His first coming brought grace that trains us to live godly lives now. His second coming is our blessed hope. In between we live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives. And Paul calls Jesus our great God and Savior, a direct statement of his deity.

6.reflection:
Why do you think the New Testament refuses to give us a date for Christ's return?

How does 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 change the way Christians grieve?

Read Titus 2:11-14. How should the hope of Christ's return shape the way you live this week?

Spend time praying "Come, Lord Jesus." What feelings or fears does that prayer stir in you?
